content: When multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) or small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) were included three times per week, they significantly reduced the iron deficiency gap, providing 96% and 84% of the Nutrient Reference Value (NRV) for iron, respectively. However, when SQ-LNS was included daily (seven days per week), a gap remained for the non-target nutrient vitamin B12, achieving only 94% of the NRV. All fortified items substantially reduced the gaps for the non-target nutrient vitamin D. For further details, refer to Annex 10. At 6-9 months of age, certain nutrients such as vitamin A, folic acid, niacin, and magnesium were not associated with tolerable upper intake levels (ULs) because the ULs apply only to synthetic forms or pharmacologic agents. For all other target and non-target nutrients, no ULs were established for infants and young children (IYC). Model solutions exceeded ULs only for copper and zinc, as shown in Annex 9. Sensitivity analyses assuming lower iron absorption revealed that the UL for zinc was exceeded in approximately half of the scenarios involving fortified items, while the UL for copper was exceeded in nearly all such scenarios. Additional details are available in Annex 10. The characteristics of food patterns in the model solutions were analyzed, including the percentage of energy intake from macronutrients, broad food groups, and specific food subgroups, as well as the frequency of consumption (daily servings). Macronutrient intakes as a percentage of energy were relatively consistent across all feasible and liberalized best-case food patterns. Low-energy food patterns had a higher percentage of energy from protein, particularly for older age groups, while liberalized patterns showed slightly higher protein and lower carbohydrate percentages. For infants aged 9 months, macronutrient distributions across all food patterns were within recommended ranges, although no specific ranges are set for infants. Refer to Annex 9 for more details. The percentage of energy from starchy staples tended to increase with higher available kilocalories from complementary foods. At 9 months of age, starchy staples contributed a lower proportion of energy in liberalized food patterns, where more generous amounts of other food groups could be selected. Fruits contributed a higher percentage of energy as energy levels increased, particularly for non-breastfed children at low and middle energy levels. In contrast, the percentage of energy from vegetables decreased as energy levels increased, as the same number of servings was selected across all levels, often reaching the maximum allowed by model constraints. Dairy contributed a low percentage of energy (0-6%) at 9 months of age, with the highest contribution observed in non-breastfed children, although this decreased as energy levels increased. Protein foods showed a marked decrease in energy contribution across energy levels for 9-month-old children, reflecting the model's minimization of protein once nutrient targets were met. Added fats and oils were not included in food patterns for breastfed infants, and their contribution was low (2%) at low energy intake levels, increasing substantially at higher energy levels. The modeled food patterns included a diverse selection of food subgroups, with some subgroups selected at maximum levels. For example, dark green leafy vegetables, liver, and small fish consumed with bones were consistently selected at maximum levels across multiple solutions. Other subgroups, such as peppers, tomatoes, immature peas/beans, and soy foods, were selected in fewer solutions. Diversity was generally lower in liberalized models, where larger amounts of individual subgroups could be selected. Most solutions included three of the five main food groups and five to seven of the eight infant and young child feeding (IYCF) indicator food groups. For starchy staples, the minimum possible quantity was selected in most scenarios, with whole grain breakfast cereals being the only subgroup consistently chosen. Fruits were included in all feasible food patterns but were excluded from liberalized patterns when other food groups (e.g., vegetables, protein foods) were available in larger quantities. Added fats and oils were not selected in any food patterns. Protein foods and vegetables were consistently included, with a wide variety of subgroups represented, including both animaland plant-based sources.
